confirmed.title: rateLimits, webhookEvents and cache/** have NO explicit rule — secured only by Firestore's implicit default-deny, unlike config/audit which are explicit `if false`
confirmed.where: firestore.rules — absent: match /rateLimits/**, match /webhookEvents/**, match /cache/** (only /config and /audit at L44,L50 are explicit)
confirmed.scenario: These server-only collections (rateLimits/{uid}__*, webhookEvents/{id}) and the shared market caches (cache/universe, cache/trending) are currently unreachable by clients — the live probe confirmed every read/list DENIED. But they rely on the implicit default-deny of an unmatched path rather than an explicit `allow read, write: if false;`. This is not exploitable today (Firestore never fails open on an unmatched path), but it is inconsistent with the file's own 'explicit rule per path' discipline and would silently become world-open the day anyone adds a broad `match /{document=**}` catch-all.
confirmed.fixIdea: Add explicit deny blocks for defense-in-depth and clarity: `match /rateLimits/{document=**} { allow read, write: if false; }`, same for `/webhookEvents/**` and (currently) `/cache/**`. cache contains only shared public market data (metadata/price/volume/supply/trending) — no per-user data — so keeping it proxy-only + explicit-deny is the correct posture.

confirmed.title: users create/update shape is NOT closed (no hasOnly) — an owner can write arbitrary extra top-level fields to their OWN user doc

confirmed.scenario: The create rule blocklists privileged keys (subscription/billingCycle/tierBeforeFailure/paypalSubscriptionId/premiumLimits/deleted/deletedAt) and requires tier=='free', and the update rule blocks those plus tier/joined — but neither uses a `hasOnly` allowlist. Live probe wrote a 2000-char `junkField` on create AND a `junk2` field on update to the caller's own /users doc, both ALLOWED. Also `joined` is not in the create blocklist, so a fake join date can be set at signup. Impact is confined to the user's OWN document (no cross-tenant leak) and bounded by the 1 MB doc size, so it is a data-hygiene / potential free-storage weakness, not an isolation hole — but it contradicts the rule comment's 'closed, typed shape' claim (only name/settings/consent are shape-checked; unknown top-level keys pass).

confirmed.title: isAdmin() uses `request.auth.token.admin == true`, which raises a rules evaluation error for tokens lacking the claim — fails safe (deny) but is a fragile idiom
confirmed.where: firestore.rules L37-39 isAdmin(); used in every read/update/delete rule (L98,127,138,146,157,160,168,179,181,189,196,198,209,211)
confirmed.scenario: For a signed-in user WITHOUT the admin custom claim, evaluating `request.auth.token.admin` on a token missing that key produces the emulator error 'Property admin is undefined on object.' In every place isAdmin() is used it is combined with isOwner via `||` (reads/delete) or with a blocked-field owner branch, so the net result is a correct DENY for non-owners and a correct ALLOW for owners (the error branch never flips a result open — the live probe confirmed all cross-tenant reads and privileged writes DENIED). Real admins carry the claim so isAdmin() returns true normally. No isolation impact, but the error-raising access is brittle.
confirmed.fixIdea: Use the null-safe idiom `request.auth.token.get('admin', false) == true` in isAdmin() to avoid the evaluation error while preserving identical allow/deny behavior.
confirmed.repro: Emulator logged 'Property admin is undefined on object. for update @ L127' during the privileged-write probes, yet those writes were correctly DENIED and legitimate owner writes were ALLOWED — errors never failed open.

confirmed.title: users/{uid} profile doc is not closed-shape: a user can persist admin:true / isAdmin:true / role into their OWN profile
confirmed.where: firestore.rules — users update rule L127-136 (and create L104-114); validUserData L221-223 only checks `name`
confirmed.scenario: Any signed-in user calls updateDoc(users/<theirUid>, {admin:true, isAdmin:true, role:'superuser', junk:'...'}) and it is stored. The owner-update rule guards privileged writes with a blocklist — affectedKeys().hasAny(['tier','joined','deleted','deletedAt','premiumLimits','subscription','billingCycle','tierBeforeFailure','paypalSubscriptionId']) — which does NOT include admin/isAdmin/role or any unknown key, so those pass. Today the injected fields grant nothing (every authorization decision reads the signed custom claim, never a Firestore field), but admin/user separation now rests entirely on the invariant that no code ever trusts a users-doc admin/isAdmin/role field. The moment any future path does — a client-side admin gate, an admin-panel display that trusts the profile row instead of customClaims, a rule that reads the profile — this becomes a self-serve privilege escalation with zero server involvement.
confirmed.fixIdea: Close the shape: add `request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys().hasOnly([<allowed owner-writable keys: name, settings, consent, portfolioCount, ...>])` to the users update rule, and an equivalent `request.resource.data.keys().hasOnly([...])` to the create rule, so unknown keys (admin/isAdmin/role/junk) are rejected. This also removes the incidental storage-abuse vector (arbitrary large fields in one's own doc, only name is size-capped) and makes 'a new field is privileged-by-default' the safe default (see finding 2). Add a rules test.
confirmed.repro: Live emulator (throwaway non-admin user): updateDoc injecting {admin:true,isAdmin:true,role:'superuser',junk:200chars} => ALLOWED and read back intact. Same user: getStats/listUsers/setAdminClaim => functions/permission-denied; getDoc(config/app)/getDoc(audit/*) => permission-denied; getIdTokenResul

confirmed.title: Admin/billing-controlled per-user fields are co-located inside the user-owned users/{uid} doc, protected only by an enumerated blocklist
confirmed.where: firestore.rules users update rule L127-136; fields tier/joined/deleted/deletedAt/premiumLimits/subscription/billingCycle/tierBeforeFailure/paypalSubscriptionId written by Admin-SDK callables in functions/index.js
confirmed.scenario: The founder goal is per-user + admin data separation. criticAdds.title: Backup / PITR / scheduled-export is a single un-partitioned tenancy surface that right-to-erasure never reaches
criticAdds.where: firebase.json (no firestore backup/export config), functions/index.js:577 recursiveDelete + :1070 purgeExpiredTrash + deleteMyAccount — all operate on the live DB only; single (default) database holds users/**, config/**, audit/** together
criticAdds.scenario: Every tenant's holdings PLUS the walled-off config/app secrets doc and the PII-bearing audit collection live in ONE Firestore database, so any Managed Backup, Point-in-Time-Recovery window, or scheduled BigQuery/GCS export is whole-database granularity — there is no per-tenant export boundary, and whoever can read the export bucket / restore a backup reads all users + admin config at once. Worse for erasure: soft-delete, purgeExpiredTrash, and deleteUser's recursiveDelete only touch the live DB — a user who exercised right-to-erasure still exists in full in every backup/PITR snapshot and every export taken before purge, with no scrub path. The whole audit considered only within-DB residue (audit/rateLimits) and never this out-of-DB copy surface.
criticAdds.evidence: No backup/export/PITR config in repo; grep for exportDocuments/pointInTime/gs:// = none; all three erasure paths target db.collection('users') only.
criticAdds.fixIdea: Document the backup/export/PITR retention as part of the tenancy model; set a bounded PITR/backup retention; add erased-user handling to the export pipeline (or note it as an accepted, disclosed retention window in the privacy policy) so a purge is eventually reflected in derived copies.

criticAdds.title: Cloud Functions runtime service account has project-wide god-mode — per-tenant AND admin-vs-user isolation rests entirely on app-code guards with zero infra least-privilege
criticAdds.where: functions/index.js:42 admin.initializeApp() (default creds, no runWith/serviceAccount anywhere — grep runWith/serviceAccount = none)
criticAdds.scenario: The functions runtime uses the default GCF/App Engine service account with the Admin SDK, which BYPASSES all Firestore rules. That single identity can read/write every tenant's subtree and the deny-by-default config/** (Anthropic + PayPal secrets) and audit/** collections. So the entire per-tenant boundary and the admin-data-separated-from-users property are enforced only by the guard-first isAdminToken/self-uid checks in application code — no defense-in-depth. One missing guard, one injection into the /api proxy, or one over-broad new callable escalates directly to full cross-tenant + admin-secret compromise, and the audit's 'all callables guard-first' confirmation is the ONLY thing standing between a bug and total breach.
criticAdds.evidence: No runWith({serviceAccount}) or minimal-role IAM binding; admin.initializeApp() with default credentials; Admin SDK inherently bypasses rules.
criticAdds.fixIdea: Run functions under a dedicated least-privilege service account (only the Firestore/Auth/Secret Manager scopes actually used); move secrets to Secret Manager with per-function grants; treat the guard checks as the app layer, not the only layer.

criticAdds.title: Admin-claim revocation and user suspension are not token-revoked and no callable uses checkRevoked — stale privileged authority for up to ~1h
criticAdds.where: functions/index.js:434 setAdminClaim (no revokeRefreshTokens on demote) · :555 suspendUser updateUser({disabled}) (no revoke) · revokeRefreshTokens exists only at :625/:678 · isAdminToken :61 reads token.admin with no checkRevoked
criticAdds.scenario: Demoting a rogue/compromised admin (setCustomUserClaims {admin:false}) does NOT revoke their tokens, and callables verify the presented ID token without checkRevoked — so the demoted admin's cached token still carries {admin:true} and passes every isAdminToken gate (getStats/listUsers/setUserTier/deleteUser/setAdminClaim/saveConfig...) for up to ~1h after the remediation. Same root cause hits containment: suspendUser only sets Auth disabled, so a suspended abuser keeps a valid ID token and can still read/write their own Firestore subtree until the token expires; and signOutEverywhere's revokeRefreshTokens doesn't tear down a second device's already-open onSnapshot streams or its unexpired access token, so live per-user data keeps flowing on the other device for the token's remaining lifetime. Revocation is treated as immediate everywhere in the UX but is actually eventual.
criticAdds.evidence: grep revokeRefreshTokens = only lines 625, 678; setAdminClaim (434) and suspendUser (555) omit it; no checkRevoked/verifyIdToken(...,true) anywhere.
criticAdds.fixIdea: Call admin.auth().revokeRefreshTokens(uid) inside setAdminClaim (both grant and revoke) and suspendUser; for the ~1h access-token window on the most sensitive admin callables, verify with checkRevoked (or a short custom-claim epoch) so demote/suspend take effect immediately.
